chunks: "Because the loop is part of the circuit you're measuring, and its size sets how much it distorts the measurement. There are three effects, and they all scale with loop size.
First, inductance. A loop's inductance grows with its size, roughly a nanohenry per millimetre of lead.
That inductance is in series with the probe's capacitance, so it makes a resonance, f equals one over two pi root LC.
With 150 nanohenries and 10 picofarads it's about 130 megahertz and fairly underdamped, so a fast edge rings.
Shrink the loop to a spring tip of around 10 nanohenries and the ring goes up to 500 megahertz and is damped. Second, pickup.
By Faraday's law, a changing magnetic field through the loop induces a voltage proportional to the loop area.
If the loop is 80 times bigger in area, it picks up 80 times more from, say, a nearby switch node.
With a 100 milliamp, 5 nanosecond edge five centimetres away, a 10 by 2 centimetre loop would see around 160 millivolts, while a 5 by 5 millimetre loop sees about 2 millivolts.
That's the difference between thinking you have a noise problem and not. Third, a long return path shares copper with other currents and also radiates and receives more EMI.
So a small loop gives a more accurate waveform, with real rise time, real overshoot and real noise.
That's why I use a spring tip or tip-and-barrel at a ground pad right next to the signal."
